name: Scalp microneedling roller

lead: A scalp microneedling roller, or derma roller, is a handheld barrel of short needles rolled across the scalp to make tiny punctures. Hair-loss communities use it together with topical minoxidil aiming for denser hair and a stronger minoxidil response.

The tiny injuries are thought to trigger a wound-healing response that releases growth factors, activates follicular stem cells and improves absorption of topicals. A 2013 randomized, evaluator-blinded pilot of 100 men reported a larger hair-count gain at 12 weeks when weekly clinic microneedling was added to 5% minoxidil than with minoxidil alone. That trial used clinician-applied treatment, not low-cost home rollers.

paras: Home users roll the device over the thinning scalp on a regular schedule, with consumer needle lengths of roughly 0.25 to 1.0 mm, and apply minoxidil as part of the routine. Clinics offer longer-needle sessions. Changes are tracked over months.

Reported risks include irritation, bleeding, infection from non-sterile or reused rollers, and cross-contamination if shared. Rollers need cleaning and replacement, and no published trial of home rollers is available.

chain: Wound response and better topical absorption
angle.text: Hair-loss communities roll home derma rollers across the scalp, usually with topical minoxidil, aiming for denser hair. The tiny punctures are thought to prompt a wound response and better absorption. A 2013 pilot of 100 men studied clinic microneedling plus minoxidil; home rollers have not been trialed.

lead: A scalp microneedling roller, also called a derma roller, is a handheld barrel covered in short needles that is rolled across the scalp to make many tiny punctures. People with thinning hair use it, usually alongside topical minoxidil, hoping to thicken hair and improve scalp coverage and hairline density [1][2].

Microneedling in general, also called collagen induction therapy, skin needling or dermarolling, is a cosmetic procedure that repeatedly punctures the skin with small sterile needles; it has been used for scarring and acne, and some studies have found it paired with minoxidil more effective than minoxidil alone for androgenetic alopecia [2]. Consumer rollers are sold with needle lengths of roughly 0.25 to 1.0 mm.

The main published support is a 2013 randomized, evaluator-blinded pilot study from India in 100 men. It reported a larger hair-count increase at 12 weeks when weekly microneedling was added to 5% minoxidil than with minoxidil alone [1]. The study tested clinician-applied treatment in a clinic, and no published trial of low-cost home rollers is available.

paras: The device is a small roller fitted with fine needles. Rolling it over skin creates microscopic channels, a procedure known as microneedling or collagen induction therapy. In hair loss, the technique is used together with topical drugs, most often minoxidil.

Proponents propose that the micro-injuries trigger a wound-healing response that releases growth factors and activates follicular stem cells, and that the channels may also increase absorption of topical drugs. How far these effects occur with the shallow needles of home devices is not established by published trials.

Microneedling is sometimes combined in clinics with platelet-rich plasma, made from the patient's own blood; Wikipedia says the efficacy of that combination remains in question pending scientific studies [2]. Wikipedia also cites a 2015 review of microneedling in skin of colour, a topic distinct from scalp use [2].

In the 2013 pilot study, 100 men with mild to moderate androgenetic alopecia were randomized to weekly microneedling plus twice-daily 5% minoxidil or to minoxidil alone, and followed for 12 weeks. Mean hair count in a fixed 1 cm2 area rose by about 91 in the microneedling group versus about 22 in the minoxidil-only group. Investigators and patients also rated the combination more favourably [1]. The authors described the work as a pilot, the follow-up was short, and the procedure was performed in a clinic with needles longer than those in most home rollers.
No published trial has tested a consumer-grade roller used by patients at home.

Because the technique breaks the skin, irritation, bleeding and infection are possible, particularly if a roller is not cleaned or is shared between people. Wikipedia notes that infection is the main concern with microneedling, citing a 2024 CDC report of three HIV diagnoses among patients of one New Mexico spa offering PRP microneedling facials, a clinical setting that differs from scalp rolling at home [2]. The cited pilot trial did not report adverse events in its abstract, and published data on adverse events from home use are limited [1].
Threads on Hair Loss Talk and the archived r/tressless community discuss dermarolling and minoxidil results and ask whether to add a roller to a regrowth routine [3][4].

lore.intro: Dermarolling is discussed in hair-loss forums as an add-on to minoxidil, with threads sharing before-and-after results and asking whether to add it [3][4].

claims.claim: A cheap home roller works like the clinic treatment
